content: Self-management education aims to assist individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) and their families in making informed decisions about treatment, monitoring their condition, and adapting their care to manage the impact of the disease on their daily lives. Although various self-management education programs have been developed for CF, no prior systematic review has evaluated the effectiveness of these interventions. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of self-management education interventions on health outcomes for individuals with CF and their caregivers. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register (last searched on August 22, 2013), as well as databases accessed through EBSCO (CINAHL, Psychological and Behavioural Sciences Collection, PsychInfo, SocINDEX) and Elsevier (Embase). Relevant journals and conference proceedings were also hand-searched, with the last search conducted on February 1, 2014. The review included randomized controlled trials, quasi-randomized controlled trials, or controlled clinical trials that compared different types of self-management education for CF or compared self-management education with standard care or no intervention. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility of trials and evaluated the risk of bias, while three authors extracted data from the included studies. Four trials, involving a total of 269 participants, were included in the review. Three trials focused on children with CF and their parents or caregivers, while one trial involved adults with CF. The interventions evaluated included: (1) a general training program for managing CF; (2) education specific to aerosol and airway clearance treatments; (3) disease-specific nutrition education; and (4) a combination of general and disease-specific nutrition education. The results showed that training children to manage CF in general did not lead to statistically significant changes in weight after six to eight weeks, with a mean difference of -7.74 lb (approximately -3.51 kg) and a 95% confidence interval ranging from -35.18 to 19.70. Similarly, general and disease-specific nutrition education for adults did not result in statistically significant improvements in pulmonary function (measured as forced expiratory volume in one second, FEV1), weight, or dietary fat intake scores at six or 12 months. For example, the mean difference in FEV1 was -5.00% (95% CI: -18.10 to 8.10) at six months and -5.50% (95% CI: -18.46 to 7.46) at 12 months. Weight changes were minimal, with a mean difference of -0.70 kg (95% CI: -6.58 to 5.18) at six months and -0.70 kg (95% CI: -6.62 to 5.22) at 12 months. Dietary fat intake scores also showed no significant changes, with a mean difference of 1.60 (85% CI: -2.90 to 6.10) at six months and 0.20 (95% CI: -4.08 to 4.48) at 12 months. There is limited evidence suggesting that self-management education may improve knowledge in patients with CF, but not in their parents or caregivers. Additionally, there is some evidence indicating that self-management education may lead to small positive changes in certain behaviors among both patients and caregivers. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient in both quantity and quality to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of self-management education for CF. Further research is needed to explore the impact of self-management education on a broader range of clinical and behavioral outcomes in children, adolescents, and adults with CF, as well as their caregivers.
